newsitem.title: USA: Trie had complex money laundering scheme, says FBI.
newsitem.headline: Trie had complex money laundering scheme, says FBI.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

An FBI agent laid out for a U.S. Senate committee on Tuesday how former Little Rock restaurant owner Yah Lin "Charlie" Trie set up a web of shell companies which laundered money from an Asian business associate and donated more than $220,000 to the Democratic National Committee.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee investigating campaign fund-raising scandals heard from special agent Jerome Campane about the murky activities of Trie, who himself has taken refuge in China and refused to testify.
The committee is investigating how foreign money, mostly from Asian business interests, illegally flowed into 1996 political campaigns and whether U.S. security was damaged or favours bought.
The hearings have had little political impact, partly because the material is complex and the names are foreign.

The committee heard evidence culled from subpoenaed bank records of how Trie received $905,000 from a Macau-based business tycoon called Ng Lap Sing, whom Campane and others on the committee referred to by his Mandarin name, Mr. Wu.

The money flowed through six separate accounts established by Trie under a variety of different corporate names. Sometimes he switched funds from account to account several times before it finally wound up in Democratic coffers.

Wu was anxious to attend a fund raising dinner at a Washington hotel in February, 1996 addressed by Clinton, apparently hoping to have his photograph taken with the president, which might boost his status back home.
The committee heard from two Chinese housewives who live in Maryland who said they wrote checks to the DNC totalling $25,000 so that Mr. Wu could gain admittance to the dinner.
The two, Yue Chu and Xi Ping Wang, testified through an interpreter after they were granted immunity from prosecution.

Yue Chu, whose husband works for Mr. Wu in Beijing, wrote two checks totalling $20,000. Xi Ping Wang, whose husband is Ms. Chu's husband's cousin, wrote one for $5,000. Both were immediately reimbursed by Mr. Wu's Washington representative, Keshi Zhan.
"I thought I was going to help the boss to buy the ticket to pass the gate," Ms. Chu said.

Along with his wife and company, Trie gave more than $200,000 to the Democratic Party from 1994 to 1996 and $600,000 to President Bill Clinton's Presidential Legal Expense Trust. The money was returned when it became clear it came from overseas.

Trie got his start as owner of a Chinese restaurant often frequented by Clinton, who was then governor of Arkansas, and others who went on to work at the White House after Clinton was elected president in 1992.
He transferred his activities to Washington D.C. around 1992, apparently hoping to turn his personal relations with government officials into business opportunities.
But Campane said Trie turned out to be a poor businessman. He enjoyed the high life, playing the genial host to visiting Asian businessmen. But he never made money.
At some point, Trie became the conduit for money from Mr. Wu, who emerged from the testimony as a shadowy figure whose motives remained unclear.

Campane said he had no evidence either that Trie's money came through Mr. Wu from the Chinese government in an effort to influence U.S. foreign policy, or that Clinton or the Democratic Party knew the money Trie donated came from overseas, which was illegal.
Trie did visit the White House at least 23 times and was in frequent contact on the telephone with Mark Middleton, who was special assistant to the president.
Republican senators made much of the fact that Mr. Wu, had been described in news reports as a member of a commission that advised the Chinese government and the Communist Party on business affairs.
That virtually made him a Chinese government official, said Pennsylvania Republican Arlen Specter.
But Democrat Sen. Richard Durbin of Illinois said it proved little. "Those who want to make out of this a Chinese plot still have a lot of evidence to bring," he said.
